questions.question: What is a narrative's plot?
choices: The sequence and connection of events
A list of character traits
The author's purpose statement
A description of the setting only

questions.question: Which detail most effectively establishes a tense setting?
choices: Mina was a student
The hallway lights flickered as a locked door clicked behind Mina
The school had three floors
It was Tuesday

questions.question: A story's conflict is best described as
choices: the lesson stated in the title
a list of places in the story
a central problem or tension that drives events
the narrator's vocabulary

questions.question: Why might a writer begin a story in the middle of an important action?
choices: To avoid developing any characters
To explain every event before the story begins
To remove the need for a setting
To create immediate momentum and raise questions for the reader

questions.question: Which choice best reveals a character indirectly?
choices: He folded the map twice before handing it back without speaking
He was nervous
The character's name was Sam
The story takes place in a city

questions.question: A narrator describes events as 'I' and knows only their own thoughts. What point of view is this?
choices: Second person
First person
Third-person omniscient
Third-person limited

questions.question: What is a turning point in a narrative?
choices: The first descriptive sentence
A repeated character trait
An event that changes the direction or stakes of the story
A detail unrelated to the conflict

questions.question: A writer wants dialogue to reveal tension. Which exchange is most effective?
choices: 'Hello,' she said. 'Hello,' he replied.
'It is Tuesday,' he said. 'Yes,' she said.
'The sky is blue,' she said. 'It is.'
'You said you locked it.' 'I thought you did.'

questions.question: Why should a writer vary sentence length in a narrative?
choices: Pacing and emphasis can change with the action or reflection
Every sentence must have a different subject
Long sentences are always more descriptive
Short sentences remove the need for plot

questions.question: A story's resolution should generally
choices: introduce every character for the first time
show how the central conflict is addressed or left changed
repeat the opening without change
add a new conflict unrelated to the story

questions.question: A writer describes a character's hands shaking before an audition. What does this detail most directly do?
choices: Explain the entire plot
Establish the story's historical period
Suggest emotion through physical behavior
Prove the narrator knows every thought

questions.question: Which transition best signals a flashback?
choices: At the same time, the train arrived
She closed the door
The station was crowded
Two years earlier, the same station had been their meeting place

questions.question: A narrative has many events but no clear focus. What should the writer do?
choices: Select events that develop the central conflict or character change
Add more unrelated scenes
Remove the setting
Replace all actions with definitions

questions.question: What is foreshadowing?
choices: A return to an earlier event
A clue that hints at a later event
A direct statement of the theme
A description of the setting

questions.question: A narrator says, 'I never worry,' while nervously checking the window every minute. What can the contrast reveal?
choices: The setting is a courtroom
The story has no conflict
The narrator's actions may contradict their words
The narrator is omniscient

questions.question: Which ending creates the strongest sense of character development?
choices: The story stops in the middle of a sentence
A new character appears without context
The conflict disappears without explanation
The character makes a choice that shows a changed understanding

questions.question: What should a writer consider when choosing a narrative point of view?
choices: Which perspective best serves the story's information and effect
Which pronoun appears most often in the title
Whether the story has a dialogue line
How many pages the draft will be

questions.question: A scene feels rushed. Which revision is most likely to improve it?
choices: Add a summary of unrelated events
Develop the key moment with action, sensory detail, and character response
Remove the central choice
Explain the ending before the scene

questions.question: Why is a specific detail usually more effective than a general one?
choices: It guarantees the story is true
It eliminates the need for sequence
It helps the reader imagine the scene and infer meaning
It makes every character identical

questions.question: A writer wants the climax to feel earned. What should earlier scenes do?
choices: Hide all relevant information until after the ending
Include only background description
Avoid introducing the central conflict
Develop causes, stakes, and choices that lead toward it
